book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

chapters.file: ch24 - 13. How to Be a Dwarf.md
chapters.relation: Using Carrot (a human raised in a dwarf mine who is accepted as a dwarf), Cheery Littlebottom (an openly female dwarf), and Gladys the golem, the chapter argues that social identity is neither biology nor a one-time choice but an ongoing performance that must also be recognized by insiders and outsiders. It applies de Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' to Cheery's creation of a female dwarf gender against the deep-downers' equality that treats every dwarf as male, and reads the black ribboners versus the Magpyrs as assimilation versus doubling down on identity. Essentialist outsiders like Fred Colon and the Campaign for Equal Heights fail because they cling to stereotypes when individuals like Cheery or Carrot do not fit the mold, while Vetinari's indifference and Mrs. Cake's accommodations leave identity to those who must choose and perform it.

chapters.file: ch25 - 14. Being One’s Me (Witchy) Personal Identity on the Discworld.md
chapters.relation: The chapter reads Granny Weatherwax's analysis of Magrat—'you're your me'—through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, opening with Granny's broomstick, whose stick and bristles the dwarf engineers have replaced dozens of times yet which remains 'the same' broomstick, as a Theseus's-ship puzzle for witches. It stages Locke's view against the classic objections: Butler's circularity charge that memory presupposes identity, and fission worries raised by the duplicated Glods of Al-Ybi and by the mirror magic that splits Granny and Lilith among a billion reflections. Death's challenge to each witch to find 'the one that's real' in the mirror universe becomes the test case, and Granny's simply looking down at herself and saying 'This one' is offered as a vindication of a Butlerian, body-anchored and indefinable conception of personal identity.

chapters.file: ch26 - IV. Ye Canna’ Ken What Ye Canna’ Ken.md
ch27 - 15. The Serious Monk’s Guide to Re-writing History.md
chapters.relation: Framed as a monkey monk-to-be telling four bored children the 'history' of four Discworld novels, the chapter argues that history is not a record of what happened but a constructed narrative: in Wyrd Sisters the Duchess commissions Hwel's play to rewrite the murder of the king, since 'the past is what people remember, and memories are words.' In Small Gods, Brutha's photographic memory of Ephebe's burning library shows that even perfect recollection is lost unless written down, while in Thief of Time the History Monks openly rebuild time as a patchwork after the Big Crash, and Susan watches historians 'rebuilt the image of the past to suit the eyesight of today.' Drawing on W. H. Walsh's idea of history as intelligible narrative, it concludes that history is performative—what people are told it is—and that we ourselves are the crowbar that opens the box of history from the inside.

The chapter sets out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge with Discworld examples—Archchancellor Ridcully as a fallible authority, the physics of thaum particles as coherentist justification—before constructing a Discworld Gettier case in which a young wizard sees a fake level-seven wizard killed and truly but accidentally reports that 'a level seven wizard was killed.' It then tests the standard repairs, applying Nozick's truth-tracking function and Goldman's causation function to a case where a man blames the notorious Reacher Gilt for a theft actually committed by the dwarf he bumped into, and argues that neither truth-tracking nor specificity makes the problem go away. The upshot is that Discworlders, used to expecting to be wrong, may let go of false 'knowledge' more easily than our confidently wrong Roundworld.

chapters.file: ch29 - 17. Sin, My Young Man, Is When You Treat People as Things.md
chapters.relation: Taking Granny Weatherwax's definition that sin 'is when you treat people as things' and Vetinari's that sin is not saying no to evil, the chapter reads Discworld through C. S. Lewis's argument that a universal Law of Human Nature—felt on the Disc by dwarfs, trolls, and even atheists—points to a divine lawgiver. The enchanted wolf in Witches Abroad, whose agony every witch intuits as wrong and who is granted a merciful death and human funeral, shows that shared moral intuition at work, and grounds the chapter's notes on Pratchett's own campaign for assisted dying. Finally, the Assassins' Guild, which only inhumes the rich who can afford bodyguards under its motto nil mortifi sine lucre, illustrates John Paul II's 'structures of sin': killing sanctified by contract and city law, treating people as things.

chapters.file: ch31 - 18. Fate on the Discworld and Roundworld.md
chapters.relation: Written as a dialogue in which Death visits the sweeper Lu-Tze, the chapter distinguishes Discworld fate—narrativium and narrative causality, where million-to-one chances come off and Mort's attempt to save a princess bounced back into an alternative timeline—from the Roundworld debates about determinism. Epicurus's swerving atom, the Stoic compatibilism of Chrysippus (choices flowing from one's own beliefs and desires, which Death admits he prefers), Carneades's 'voluntary motion of the mind' and his truth-without-necessity solution to future contingents, and Augustine and Boethius on desire-based choice and God's atemporal foreknowledge are all worked through. The Disc's changeable past—Dios traveling back to found Djelibeybi, Rincewind's sandwich seeding life, Vimes in his own past—is what motivates Carneades's distinction between truth and necessity, and the Stoic line that fate can work through the witches' own free choices.

chapters.file: ch32 - 19. The Alchemy of Flat Worlds.md
chapters.relation: Staged as Professor Moby Dickens Melville's 'Philosophy of Worlds' course uniting Discworld wizards with the geometric Flatlanders of Abbott's novella, the chapter contrasts a storytelling, narrative-causality philosophy of Discworld with Flatland's mathematical, hierarchy-obsessed rationalism, and extends the contrast to physics (wizards favor loop quantum gravity, Flatlanders string theory) and theology (Hex's self-designed universe and words of power versus Flatland's circle-priests who rule women declared 'deficient in Reason'). When a Flatlander woman, Ms. Transversal, protests that calling the new softer approach 'feminine' repeats Abbott's sexism, the class closes with the narrator's suggestion, from a chalk-nub's-eye view, that everything we know may reflect the direction from which we see rather than the truth itself.

chapters.file: ch33 - 20. The Intersection of Science and Philosophy, the Seediest Corner in Ankh-Morpork.md
chapters.relation: A comic sprint through Western thought anchored in the Science of Discworld books, the chapter runs from Aristotle—whose geocentric four-element physics, it notes, fits Discworld better than Roundworld, and whose condemnations of usury it digresses over—through Descartes's cogito and mind-body dualism, Ryle's 'ghost in the machine,' behaviorism, identity theory, eliminative materialism, and functionalism's brain-as-computer picture, to show how philosophy of mind advances by each theory picking on its predecessor. Newton's occult-seeming gravity, later overturned by Einstein, illustrates the chapter's real thesis drawn from Pratchett's 'Lies-to-Wizards': neither science nor philosophy erects a timeless edifice of facts, since 'every so often, you have to unlearn what you thought you already knew,' while Diogenes and the Cynics supply the model of philosophy done in the common tongue that Pratchett shares.

Built on Jakob von Uexküll's Umwelt—the 'island of the senses' that enfolds each creature, illustrated by a moth that smells only a mate's pheromone and hears only the bat's echolocation—the chapter argues that every Discworld being likewise inhabits a sliced-down life world rather than the world as a whole. The ambiguous puzuma running near light speed, dream-spinning dromes that starve victims inside stolen Umwelten, the two-dimensional Shadowing Lemma, Gaspode's pathogen-warring skin, the hermit elephant's hut, and the re-annual plant that flowers a year before its seeds each show a life world carved out by what an organism can sense and use, whether its world runs on science or magic—prompting the suggestion that the Umwelt is more fundamental than either.

chapters.file: ch35 - 22. Cocking a Snook at Death, and Getting Away with It Does the Personification of Death Make It Less Scary.md
chapters.relation: Asking whether Pratchett's personified Death makes mortality less scary, the chapter reads Reaper Man's claim that belief created Death—the moment a living thing grasped non-existence, Death came into being—as a co-arising of dualistic concepts, and surveys psychopomps from Thanatos and Azrael to Yama and even modern assisted-dying organizations. Windle Poons's several kinds of death in Reaper Man ground the distinctions between animalistic, mindistic, and personistic death, showing that whether someone counts as dead can turn on which conception of the person is doing the counting. The closing meditation on Pratchett's own posterior cortical atrophy and the documentary Choosing to Die argues that conceptualizing death in advance—in living wills and bedside conversations with loved ones—is what lets us meet 'THERE'S JUST ME' a little less afraid.

chapters.file: ch36 - 23. I’d Rather Stay an Orangutan Because That’s Why Discworld Exists.md
chapters.relation: In a self-fictionalizing chapter, editor Nicolas Michaud is summoned by Vetinari to prove Discworld is real, and the answer arrives in the Unseen University library: the Librarian stays an orangutan because language distances us from experience—humans never simply experience a banana, only 'holding a banana,' so for us the words create the reality. Along the way the chapter takes issue with Hume's bundle-of-perceptions view of the self, since word-using humans are never just a collection of present perceptions, and contrasts the Librarian's immediate, unmediated experience of each singular thing with our word-reduced world. It concludes that because we always experience the world as stories, narratives, and terms, 'narratives are all we have,' making the Disc no less real than the Roundworld we talk and think about.

holes.name: Joseph Butler
holes.what: An eighteenth-century Anglican bishop who argued that consciousness of past actions merely reveals personal identity rather than constituting it, so identity is basic, indefinable, and presupposes the persistence of the person.
holes.why: Chapter 14 builds its reading of Granny Weatherwax's 'you're your me' and 'This one' around Butler's circularity objection to Locke's memory theory and his lack of worry about duplication cases.

holes.name: History as Narrative Construction
holes.what: The narrativist thesis (associated with philosophers of history like W. H. Walsh) that history is not the past itself but an intelligible narrative constructed by historians, so the past becomes what people are told it is.
holes.why: Chapter 15's central claim—that the Duchess rewrites history through Hwel's play and the History Monks patch time as 'a patchwork, really'—is exactly this narrativist thesis, for which the taxonomy has no slug.

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: A Christian apologist whose moral argument holds that a universal Law of Human Nature, shared across cultures and felt even by unbelievers, is best explained by a divine moral lawgiver.
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds its whole account of Discworld sin on Lewis's natural-law moral argument, from shared intuitions about the enchanted wolf to the conclusion that God wrote the moral law into every creature.

holes.name: Structures of Sin
holes.what: John Paul II's notion that personal sins consolidate into social structures that spread, become self-perpetuating, and make further sin easier, so evil becomes embedded in law and custom.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses the concept explicitly to read the Assassins' Guild, whose contract-sanctioned, tax-paying killing of the rich embodies sin sanctified by city law.

holes.name: Eliminative Materialism
holes.what: The view that mature neuroscience will eliminate our commonsense folk-psychological entities—beliefs, desires, fears—leaving only brain processes as the whole story about the mind.
holes.why: Chapter 20 gives eliminative materialism its own section, explaining folk psychology through The Science of Discworld and setting it in the progression away from Descartes's dualism.

holes.name: Functionalism (Philosophy of Mind)
holes.what: The theory that mental states should be defined by their functional roles, with the brain as hardware and the mind as software, rather than by what they are made of.
holes.why: Chapter 20 closes its survey of theories of consciousness with functionalism's computer metaphor and its identification with scientism, the claim that science alone explains the mind.

holes.name: Umwelt (Life World)
holes.what: Jakob von Uexküll's notion that each organism inhabits a species-specific perceptual world, a sensory island carved out of reality by what its body can detect and use.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire reading of Discworld creatures—the moth, the ambiguous puzuma, dromes, the re-annual plant—is organized around the Umwelt concept, for which no taxonomy slug exists.
